label: Website property (static site with generated media)
summary: A static website that presents a company or product, built as original, stylized pages with art, icons, video and motion made through the media pipeline, and run locally in a container first. Not a template site.
planner_text: This is a website property: static pages in plain HTML, CSS and JavaScript that must look original and finished, not like a template. Plan these stories in this order. First a design direction story on a route that can look at images: it reads the concept images in the folder and writes DESIGN.md (palette tokens, page skeleton, type, ornament, motion, asset list). Then the build stories (theme and transitions, pages, art and icons as SVG and CSS, glass and overlays, wiring the media slots) which restyle the existing template rather than start over. Generated stills, illustrations and video come from the media pipeline run by the operator in MCD, never from an agent, so plan that as a human story after the wiring story; the site must look complete on its fallbacks before the files arrive. After the build, plan a verification story (mode read) that checks the files themselves: promised files exist and are not empty, every asset is referenced, no external requests, both themes render without console errors, reduced motion is honored. Then a preview checkpoint story (mode read) that serves the folder on localhost only and hands the operator clickable URLs per page and theme with the stop command; then a human story to approve the look, with changes going back through verification and preview. Container and pipeline files come after the pages exist and must copy the assets folder; building and running the image belongs only to a final human local verification story. A contact form handler stores only a redacted line and has a test that fails if the redaction is removed. Nothing in the folder may contain secrets or real visitor data, and no franchise names, logos or assets are used. Never ask an agent story to render pages, check a browser console or take screenshots: agent sandboxes have no browser, so keep agent verification static and leave rendering to the human preview. Put the owner's product facts (which products are live with their addresses, which are beta) in the design direction story, and give it a style decision: one visual language, with the hero still generated and approved first and used as the style reference for every other picture; cards are 16:9 photographic stills, never mixed with illustration, and clips are wide establishing shots. Add a final polish story (mode read for agents: static checks only) and a human responsive review in the preview at 1440, 1280, 1100, 1024, 768, 600, 390 and 360 pixels in both themes, looking for sideways scroll, overlapping header pieces, text spacing and art that does not fill its box, before asking for approval. Put the starting spacing, sizing and timing values from the website spacing and timing guide into DESIGN.md as tokens in the design direction story (theme crossing 1500 ms, header and card sizes, breakpoints), so the build stories use them instead of guessing. Details are in the website design guide. Background and ambient clips start on the cheapest video tier (the media panel defaults to it for this type); raise a slot to standard or premium only after looking at the result. The project ends in the remote repository, not in a scratch folder: when the brief names a repository, the working folder must be a clone of it, and the plan needs a delivery story that pushes the project branch and opens a pull request, then a story that reads the pipeline result so the image or app build and the tests have actually run there. Nothing goes to the main branch from an agent. The project is not done until the branch is pushed, the pull request is open and the pipeline result is known. The repository is private unless the site is meant to be open source: a company or product website is proprietary, so keep the code, tests and pipeline in a private repository. Say the visibility and licence in the plan. Plan the documentation as part of the project: a README story (an agent writes it) and the how-tos, with a Mermaid architecture diagram and a data-flow diagram whenever the project is more than a local install, and a screenshot of every application area plus how-tos for what a person does beyond installing and signing in. Screenshots are made with Playwright from a script kept in the repository, run by a person or a CI job against seeded test data, because agent sandboxes have no browser; the agent writes the script and the README, a human story or the pipeline runs it and commits the images. The preview checkpoint story must leave a preview script in the repository (tools/preview.sh) that serves the site with python3 -m http.server on the host's Tailscale address (from tailscale ip -4, else 127.0.0.1), a health file the site serves at /health.txt, and prints the clickable address of every page, a curl command that checks each page and /health.txt return 200, and the command to stop it, so the person can check the site from their own device. Keep the media bill small: in media/slots.json give each slot only the resolution it needs ("resolution": "1K" for a picture shown small, "480P" for a retro or VHS-look clip, which costs 0.625 of 768p and suits the look), do not generate art the code can draw (title screens inside a canvas, patterns, glows, frames), reuse one approved still as the style reference for the others, review the prompts before anything is generated, and generate one take at a time.
failure_points: A story's own report that art or media exists is not proof; generated files can be empty. Verify the files, then show them on a preview before asking a person to approve.
A container or pipeline story planned before the pages exist cannot smoke-test anything; order it after the pages.
A Dockerfile that copies only html, css and js ships a site with no assets; the container story must copy the assets folder and the smoke test must fetch an asset.
Agents cannot build or run containers: building the image, compose and the Colima checks are one final human story.
A route that cannot view images cannot follow concept art; the design direction story must run on one that can.
A human approval of how it looks has nothing to judge without a live preview and clickable URLs.
Original art only: no names, logos or assets from the concept images or any franchise; reference images stay out of the container image.
Free models cannot be trusted with taste or motion work; use a strong model for design direction, the theme engine and the transitions.

A story that asks an agent to render pages, read a browser console or take screenshots cannot be done in an agent sandbox (no browser, no loopback server); it reports itself unfinished and blocks everything behind it. Agent verification is static (files, references, syntax, tests); rendering is checked by a person in the preview.

Mixing picture styles (engraved or cartoon cards beside photographic heroes) reads as unfinished; decide one visual language in the design direction story and use the approved hero still as the style reference for every other slot.
A close-up or macro clip used as a banner background reads as a crop of rust; clips are wide establishing shots, and an ambient loop is a low-opacity blended texture over a still.
Setting an inline background-image from script replaces the layered backgrounds a theme draws and drops size and position; always set size, position and repeat with it.
A fixed grid row count that does not match the children leaves stray rows and a squashed picture; let rows follow the content.

A theme sheet's display rule outranks a plain responsive hide, so decorative plaques collide with the nav on mid-size screens; make the hide outrank the theme rule and size the breakpoints from measurements.
Product status written from guesswork (live products marked coming soon, beta products unmarked) is a content bug; record the owner's facts in the brief and update the tests that encode them.

Timing and spacing left to each build story drift: a 1-second theme crossing reads as rushed and header parts collide. Record the numbers as tokens in DESIGN.md first (see the spacing and timing guide).

A menu that only reflows at phone width, or media queries in px, break for readers with larger text: collapse the menu behind an accessible button below 760 px (visible without script) and write media queries in em.

A project run in a scratch folder with no git remote finishes with nothing pushed: no pull request and no pipeline run, so the image or app build and tests never ran where they are meant to. When the brief names a repository, the working folder must be a clone of it, and delivery (push the project branch, open the pull request, read the pipeline result) must be stories in the plan.

A README with only install commands tells a new person nothing about the application. Add a Mermaid architecture and data-flow diagram when it is more than a local install, a screenshot and a short how-to for each application area beyond installation and sign-in, and make the screenshots with a Playwright script that a person or the pipeline runs (an agent cannot run a browser).

A preview with no address to open and no way to check it is running makes the human look sign-off guesswork: leave a preview script that prints the clickable URLs (the host's Tailscale address, not localhost, when the site runs on another machine), a /health.txt and a curl check, and the stop command.

Every slot at the tier's full resolution multiplies the bill: pictures shown small do not need 2K and retro clips do not need 768p. Set a per-slot resolution, skip art the code can draw, and let the plan list each slot with its resolution and estimate before any generation.
visual_checks: Always: a file-level verification story, then a localhost preview checkpoint with clickable URLs per page and theme, then the human look sign-off. Changes loop back through verification and preview.
human_signoffs: Make the generated media in MCD (stills, clips, illustrations)
Approve the look from the live preview
Review the contact form and container stories (high risk)
Local verification on the container host (last)

checks.message: No design direction story. Start with one that reads the concept images and writes DESIGN.md.
No file-level verification story. Add one that proves the promised files exist, are not empty and are used.

No agent preview checkpoint story. An agent story should serve the folder on localhost and hand you clickable URLs, and only then should a separate human story ask for your decision, so you are never asked to approve something you cannot see.
The preview checkpoint does not follow a file verification story.
The human look approval does not come after a preview checkpoint.
The container or pipeline story is planned before the pages exist.
A story needs a container engine, which agents cannot run. Split static container files from the final human local verification story.
A container plan needs a final human runtime verification story that builds or runs the checked-out repository with Docker/Compose.
Generated media comes from the media pipeline run by the operator in MCD, not from an agent. Make it a human story.

A story asks an agent to render pages or check a browser console, which no agent sandbox can do. It will report itself unfinished. Keep agent verification to static checks and move rendering to the human preview.

No responsive and polish review. Add a human story that reviews the preview at phone, tablet and wide desktop widths in both themes for sideways scroll, overlapping header pieces, text spacing and art that does not fill its box.

No delivery story. A project should end in the remote repository: add a story that pushes the project branch and opens a pull request, and one that reads the pipeline result (the build and tests running there), or say plainly that this project has no repository.
No README or documentation story. Add one that writes the README with a Mermaid architecture and data-flow diagram (when it is more than a local install) and a how-to for each application area.

No story that makes the application screenshots. Agents cannot run a browser: add a human story (or a pipeline job) that runs the Playwright screenshot script against seeded test data and commits the images the README uses.
